title: Search Closed Sources: Threat Intel Vendors
shortTitle: Search Closed Sources: Threat Intel Vendors
summary: Commercial threat intelligence vendors publish paid reports, indicator feeds, and customer portals. The material is written for defenders, so it describes which industries are currently targeted, which tradecraft succeeds, and which countermeasures the vendor observed defeating it. An adversary who obtains access learns the same lessons, and because the reports are dated and tied to real incidents, they also show which sectors are under active focus. The artefact is entitlement rather than intrusion: a paid subscription, a trial account, or a leaked report archive. Nothing in the behaviour touches the victim, so the only records sit with the vendor. A defender can respond by reviewing what gets published, limiting environment-specific detail in shared reporting, and watching for account behaviour on their own intelligence subscriptions that does not match normal research.

beginner.definition: Threat intelligence vendors are companies that study attackers and sell reports. Their customers are defenders, such as security teams. This technique means an attacker reads or buys the same reports. The reports can show which industries are attacked and how.
beginner.whyItMatters: Reports written to help you also tell an attacker where to aim. They name the industries under attack and the tricks that still work. A patient attacker reads them and copies what succeeds. Readers are also a signal, because a new account that only downloads old reports may not be a real customer. If you publish incident detail, remember that your attacker may read it too.
howItWorks: The attacker subscribes to a vendor feed, starts a trial, or obtains a leaked report.
They read the reports for target industries, tradecraft, and successful entry methods.
They note which countermeasures defeated earlier attacks and then plan ways around them.
They compare vendor claims with public reporting to judge which sources are reliable.
They may also watch for mentions of their own activity, which is a separate technique.
They apply these lessons when they build and run their next campaign.
beginner.example: Think of a football team that buys the scouting reports written for its rivals. The reports say which defenders are slow and which play always scores. The team does not need to spy on the pitch, because the report already told it where to run. Vendor intelligence works like that. It is written for defence and read by both sides.
takeaways: Treat published threat reports as material an attacker can read too.
Watch for unusual downloads or new accounts on your intelligence portal.
Avoid naming your own live weaknesses in reporting you share.

objectives: Explain what threat intelligence vendors sell and to whom they sell it.
Describe how a report written for defenders also helps an adversary.
Explain why vendor report reading produces almost no victim telemetry.
Recognise access anomalies on your own intelligence subscriptions.
Decide which details to keep out of shared incident reporting.
